result.scope_note: The 2019 redefinition of the SI base units established the kelvin, ampere, kilogram, and mole in terms of fundamental constants. The base unit for electric current is the ampere, not the kelvin. The claim conflates the kelvin (thermodynamic temperature) with the ampere (electric current).

explanation.text: The 2019 SI defines electric current's base unit as ampere, not kelvin. Kelvin is the base unit of thermodynamic temperature.
NIST and Wikipedia sources consistently list ampere as the SI base unit for electric current and kelvin as the SI base unit for thermodynamic temperature, with no linkage between them.
Conflicting evidence shows some sources list seven base units with distinct assignments; none associate kelvin with electric current.

The kilogram, kelvin, and mole were also redefined. The text does not state that electric current has the kelvin as its base unit.

excerpts.text:
In November 2018, however, the redefinition of the ampere ― along with three other [SI base units](https://www.nist.gov/si-redefinition/definitions-si-base-units): the kilogram (mass), kelvin (temperature) and mole (amount of substance) ― was approved. Starting on May 20, 2019, the ampere is based on a fundamental physical constant: the elementary charge (e), which is the amount of electric charge in a single electron (negative) or proton (positive).

The ampere is a measure of the amount of electric charge *in motion per unit time*― that is, electric current.
One ampere is the current in which one coulomb of charge travels across a given point in 1 second.

assessment.rationale: Spans 35 and 36 state that starting May 20, 2019, the ampere is based on the elementary charge e, and is a measure of electric charge in motion per unit time. The kelvin is not mentioned as a base unit for electric current.
assessment.provenance_note: NIST page states ampere redefinition uses elementary charge e, not kelvin.
limitations: Source does not state base unit relationships explicitly

excerpts.text: The [International System of Units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_System_of_Units "International System of Units") (SI) specifies the absolute scale for measuring temperature, and the unit of measure *[kelvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin "Kelvin")* (symbol: K) for specific values along the scale.

Since the [2019 revision of the SI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_revision_of_the_SI#Kelvin "2019 revision of the SI"), the kelvin has been defined in relation to the *physical property* underlying thermodynamic temperature: the kinetic energy of atomic free particle motion.

assessment.rationale: The source defines kelvin as the unit of measurement for thermodynamic temperature and confirms the SI base unit status of kelvin. It does not state that electric current uses kelvin as its base unit.
assessment.provenance_note: Source defines kelvin and its role as SI base unit for temperature, but provides no information about electric current base units.
limitations: No mention of electric current base units
